The Gould's wattled bat, Chalinolobus gouldii, is a medium-sized vespertilionid widely distributed across mainland Australia and Tasmania. This species is well-known for its gregarious roosting habits and remarkable physiological adaptability to variable thermal environments. In laboratory-based respirometry experiments, active individuals maintained at a stable body temperature of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C] exhibited a maximum basal metabolic rate of 25.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 25.2 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the typical energetic demands of a non-torpid insectivorous bat. Neonates of this species are altricial and weigh approximately 1.9 grams [Wwb = approximately 1.9 grams] at birth, a modest size relative to the adult female, which suggests a considerable maternal energetic commitment during the early lactational period. The ultrasonic echolocation calls of this species are frequency-modulated, allowing it to forage effectively in cluttered habitats. Colony sizes can vary dramatically with season, with maternity roosts containing several hundred individuals during the spring and summer months.

Studies of reproductive output under controlled thermal conditions indicate that a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter] is the norm, with females typically producing just one litter each year [F_R_i = one litter each year] when maintained at 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C]. This slow pace of reproduction is typical of many small bats, which invest heavily in each offspring over a protracted period of maternal care. The time since birth at weaning, when the young become nutritionally independent and begin to forage on their own, occurs at approximately 49 days [tx = approximately 49 days], a duration that encompasses both the suckling stage and the initial transition at a temperature of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C] to solid food. The wet weight at weaning has been recorded at 11.7 grams [Wwx = 11.7 grams], representing a substantial gain in body mass from the birth weight of 1.9 grams and reflecting the high growth efficiency supported by the mother's milk.

Gestation in Gould's wattled bat is relatively prolonged for a mammal of its size. Under a constant ambient temperature of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C], the gestation period lasts approximately 92 days [tg = approximately 92 days], which is consistent with the lengthy developmental period seen in other vespertilionids that undergo delayed fertilization or slow embryogenesis. This extended gestation is likely linked to the species' reproductive strategy of producing a single, well-developed offspring rather than a larger litter. Female bats emerge from hibernation in early spring and ovulation occurs shortly thereafter, with copulation having taken place in the preceding autumn. The ultimate wet weight, or maximum adult body mass, attained by reproductive adults is around 17.5 grams [Wwi = around 17.5 grams], with females typically reaching slightly higher masses than males during pregnancy. This body size places Chalinolobus gouldii in the medium range among Australian microchiropterans and allows for considerable nightly foraging movements.

The onset of sexual maturity in this species occurs at a comparatively advanced age relative to its small body size, reflecting a life history characterized by delayed reproduction and elevated adult survival. Puberty is reached at 365 days after birth [tp = 365 days after birth] under standard thermoneutral conditions at 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C], meaning that individuals born in one breeding season typically do not become reproductively active until the following year. This one-year delay before sexual maturation allows juveniles to acquire the necessary foraging skills and accumulate sufficient fat reserves for the winter hibernation period. The maximum recorded lifespan for Chalinolobus gouldii is approximately 2,847 days [am = approximately 2,847 days], or just under 7.8 years, based on long-term mark-recapture studies conduct at a temperature of 31.1 °C [T = 31.1 °C]ed in Victoria. This longevity is notable among bats of comparable size and likely contributes to the species' ability to maintain stable population densities across its range.

The species' ability to enter shallow torpor confers significant energetic savings during cold periods and likely contributes to its success across a wide latitudinal gradient. Ongoing field studies continue to refine estimates of age-specific survival and the ecological factors that modulate both reproductive timing and metabolic expenditure in this adaptable species.
